name: Acrocanthosaurus
description: Acrocanthosaurus atokensis was a large Early Cretaceous theropod from North America, best recognized by the tall neural spines running along its neck, back, hips, and base of the tail. These spines probably supported a thick muscular ridge rather than a thin sail, giving the animal a distinctive raised-backed silhouette. It belonged to the allosauroid/carcharodontosaurid side of theropod evolution, so it should not be imagined as a tyrannosaur-like predator. Acrocanthosaurus had a long predatory skull, strong three-fingered forelimbs, powerful hindlimbs, and a long balancing tail. Its fossils suggest a large apex predator adapted to hunting or scavenging in Early Cretaceous floodplains and woodlands.

name: Alamosaurus
description: Alamosaurus sanjuanensis was a large Late Cretaceous titanosaur from North America, living near the end of the dinosaur age. It had a long neck, huge body, long tail, and strong columnar limbs like other sauropods. Alamosaurus is important because titanosaurs were much more common in southern continents, yet this genus shows that very large sauropods also survived in North America late in the Cretaceous. It shared ecosystems with famous dinosaurs such as Tyrannosaurus rex and Triceratops.

name: Albertosaurus
description: Albertosaurus sarcophagus was a Late Cretaceous tyrannosaurid from western North America and one of the best-known albertosaurines. It shared the general tyrannosaur body plan, including a large skull, powerful jaws, small two-fingered arms, strong hindlimbs, and a long counterbalancing tail. However, Albertosaurus was generally lighter and more gracile than Tyrannosaurus rex, with a slimmer build and longer-legged appearance that suggests a more agile predator. It likely hunted large herbivorous dinosaurs and also scavenged when opportunities appeared. Fossils from Alberta provide important evidence for tyrannosaur evolution before the appearance of the extremely massive tyrannosaurines of the very end of the Cretaceous.
fossils: Over 30 individuals found in a single bonebed

name: Allosaurus
description: Allosaurus fragilis was a large Late Jurassic theropod from North America and one of the most common large predators of the Morrison Formation. It had a long, relatively narrow skull, serrated teeth, three-fingered grasping hands, strong hindlimbs, and a long tail for balance. Small horn-like ridges above the eyes helped give Allosaurus a distinctive skull profile, separating it from tyrannosaurs and other large theropods. Compared with Tyrannosaurus rex, Allosaurus was lighter, more athletic, and had longer functional forelimbs. It likely preyed on or scavenged from large herbivores such as stegosaurs and sauropods, making it a major predator in Late Jurassic ecosystems.

name: Amargasaurus
description: Amargasaurus cazaui was a small-to-medium-sized sauropod from Early Cretaceous South America and a member of the dicraeosaurid family. Unlike extremely long-necked sauropods such as Diplodocus or Mamenchisaurus, Amargasaurus had a relatively short neck and a compact body. Its most distinctive feature was a double row of tall, backward-leaning neural spines along the neck and front part of the back. These spines may have supported keratin sheaths, soft tissue, or display structures, although their exact appearance is still debated. Amargasaurus was a quadrupedal herbivore that likely browsed on low to mid-level vegetation in ancient Patagonian environments.

name: Ankylosaurus
description: Ankylosaurus magniventris was a massive armored dinosaur from Late Cretaceous North America, famous for its broad low body, heavy bony armor, and large tail club. It belonged to the ankylosaurid group, whose bodies were protected by osteoderms, plates, and knobs embedded in the skin. Ankylosaurus had a wide skull, strong beak, powerful limbs, and a stiffened tail ending in a heavy bony club that could have been used for defense against predators such as Tyrannosaurus rex. Although it is the most famous ankylosaur, no complete skeleton has been found, so some details of its armor arrangement are reconstructed using close relatives. It was a slow-moving but extremely well-defended herbivore.

name: Apatosaurus
description: Apatosaurus was a large diplodocid sauropod from the Late Jurassic Morrison Formation of North America. It had a small head, a long muscular neck, a deep and heavy torso, sturdy limbs, and an extremely long tapering tail that may have ended in a whip-like structure. Compared with Diplodocus, Apatosaurus was more robust, with a thicker neck, heavier body, and stronger limb bones. It was a quadrupedal herbivore that likely fed on vegetation using its peg-like teeth and long reach. Apatosaurus has a complicated history with Brontosaurus, but modern research generally treats them as closely related yet distinct genera rather than simply the same dinosaur.

name: Argentinosaurus
description: Argentinosaurus huinculensis was a gigantic titanosaur sauropod from the Late Cretaceous of Patagonia, Argentina. It is often considered one of the largest land animals ever discovered, although its exact size remains uncertain because the fossil material is incomplete. Known remains include enormous vertebrae, ribs, and limb elements that indicate a colossal quadrupedal herbivore with a long neck, huge body, powerful columnar limbs, and a long tail. Argentinosaurus likely lived in Cretaceous floodplain environments and fed on large quantities of vegetation. Because its skeleton is fragmentary, reconstructions should be treated cautiously and based on comparisons with better-known giant titanosaurs rather than excessive speculation.

name: Barosaurus
description: Barosaurus lentus was a Late Jurassic diplodocid sauropod from North America, known for its very long neck and long, slender body. It was closely related to Diplodocus but had different proportions, especially in the neck and vertebrae. Barosaurus likely used its long neck to browse across a wide feeding area while standing on four columnar limbs. Its fossils are important for understanding variation among diplodocid sauropods in the Morrison Formation. It should be reconstructed as elegant and elongated, not as bulky as Apatosaurus.

name: Baryonyx
description: Baryonyx walkeri was an Early Cretaceous spinosaurid theropod from Europe, best known for its long crocodile-like snout and enormous curved thumb claw. Its jaws contained many conical to finely serrated teeth suited for gripping slippery prey, and fossil evidence shows that fish formed part of its diet. Baryonyx probably lived around rivers, lakes, and wetlands, where it may have caught fish with its jaws and powerful forelimbs while also scavenging or hunting other animals. Unlike Spinosaurus, it did not have a tall sail, strongly shortened hindlimbs, or a deep paddle-like tail. Baryonyx should be understood as a semi-aquatic or water-associated predator, but not as a fully aquatic reptile.

name: Brachiosaurus
description: Brachiosaurus altithorax was a very tall Late Jurassic sauropod from North America, famous for its longer forelimbs, high shoulders, deep chest, and elevated neck posture. Its name means “arm lizard,” referring to the unusual proportion in which the front limbs were longer than the hind limbs, giving the body an upward-sloping profile. This made Brachiosaurus visually different from lower, longer sauropods such as Diplodocus and Apatosaurus. It likely browsed on high vegetation including conifers and tree ferns. Because Brachiosaurus is not known from a complete skeleton, and many older reconstructions were influenced by the related African sauropod Giraffatitan, accurate reconstructions should remain conservative.

name: Brachylophosaurus
description: Brachylophosaurus canadensis was a Late Cretaceous hadrosaur from North America, recognized by its flat paddle-like crest on the skull. It had a duck-billed beak, complex dental batteries, a deep herbivorous body, sturdy limbs, and a long muscular tail. Several well-preserved specimens, including mummified remains with skin impressions, have made Brachylophosaurus important for understanding hadrosaur soft tissue and body shape. It should be distinguished from crestless Edmontosaurus and from hollow-crested lambeosaurines such as Corythosaurus and Parasaurolophus.

name: Brontosaurus
description: Brontosaurus excelsus was a large Late Jurassic diplodocid sauropod from North America, closely related to Apatosaurus but now often treated as a distinct genus. It had a long neck, small head, heavy body, sturdy limbs, and a very long tapering tail. Brontosaurus is historically famous because its name was once considered invalid, then later revived after detailed anatomical comparisons. It was a quadrupedal herbivore that likely fed on low to mid-level vegetation in Morrison Formation ecosystems.

name: Camarasaurus
description: Camarasaurus was a common Late Jurassic sauropod from North America, especially well known from the Morrison Formation. Unlike Diplodocus, it had a shorter, deeper skull, a more compact body, and a stronger, less extremely elongated neck and tail. Its spoon-shaped teeth suggest it fed differently from peg-toothed diplodocids, likely cropping tougher vegetation. Camarasaurus is important because it is one of the most completely known sauropods, helping paleontologists understand sauropod skulls, growth, and general body anatomy.

name: Carcharodontosaurus
description: Carcharodontosaurus saharicus was a gigantic carcharodontosaurid theropod from Late Cretaceous North Africa, named for its shark-like serrated teeth. It had a long, low skull with blade-like teeth adapted for slicing flesh, a powerful neck, three-fingered forelimbs, strong hindlimbs, and a long balancing tail. Unlike Tyrannosaurus rex, it was not built around a short, deep, bone-crushing skull; instead, its skull and teeth were more suited for cutting. The fossil history of Carcharodontosaurus is complicated, and some classic North African material has been re-evaluated, so reconstructions should be cautious. It remains one of the most iconic large predators from the Cretaceous ecosystems of northern Africa.

name: Carnotaurus
description: Carnotaurus sastrei was a distinctive Late Cretaceous abelisaurid theropod from South America, best known for its short deep skull, two thick brow horns, extremely reduced arms, and long powerful legs. Unlike tyrannosaurs or allosauroids, Carnotaurus had a very narrow skull when seen from the front and a compact, lightweight body that may have been adapted for fast movement. Its skin impressions show a scaly body with varied scale patterns and no evidence of feathers. The tiny forelimbs were even more reduced than those of tyrannosaurs, making them one of its strangest features. Carnotaurus likely lived as an active predator in semi-arid Patagonian environments, hunting smaller animals and possibly scavenging when opportunities appeared.

name: Caudipteryx
description: Caudipteryx zoui was a small Early Cretaceous oviraptorosaur from China with a short skull, toothless beak, long legs, and striking feathers on its arms and tail. It was not capable of powered flight, but its plumage shows how bird-like some non-avian dinosaurs had become. Caudipteryx likely fed on a mixed diet of plants, seeds, small animals, and other available food. It is important because it combines a dinosaurian skeleton with obvious feathers, helping demonstrate that feathers evolved before flight.

name: Centrosaurus
description: Centrosaurus apertus was a Late Cretaceous centrosaurine ceratopsian from North America, recognized by its large nasal horn, short frill, and heavy quadrupedal body. Unlike Triceratops, it did not have two long brow horns, and unlike Styracosaurus, its frill lacked the same dramatic long spikes. Centrosaurus is known from large bonebeds, suggesting herd behavior or mass mortality events. It used a powerful beak and dental batteries to process vegetation in rich floodplain ecosystems of western North America.
fossils: Many skulls and skeletons from bonebeds

name: Ceratosaurus
description: Ceratosaurus nasicornis was a Late Jurassic theropod from North America, easily recognized by the prominent nasal horn on its snout, small brow ridges above the eyes, and a row of small bony osteoderms along its back. It was a medium-to-large predator, but it should not be confused with Allosaurus, which lacked the same central nose horn. Ceratosaurus had a deep skull, sharp serrated teeth, functional three-fingered hands, strong hindlimbs, and a long muscular tail. Its body plan suggests a powerful predator that lived alongside other large carnivores in the Morrison Formation. The nasal horn was probably used for display or species recognition rather than as a primary weapon.

name: Chasmosaurus
description: Chasmosaurus belli was a Late Cretaceous chasmosaurine ceratopsian from North America, especially known for its long rectangular neck frill with large openings. Unlike Triceratops, which had a shorter solid frill and larger brow horns, Chasmosaurus had a more elongated frill, a small nose horn, and relatively modest brow horns. It was a quadrupedal herbivore with a strong parrot-like beak, shearing dental batteries, sturdy limbs, and a heavy body adapted for processing tough vegetation. The large frill may have helped with display, species recognition, or social signaling. Chasmosaurus lived in ancient coastal plains and floodplain environments that supported diverse communities of ceratopsians and hadrosaurs.

name: Coelophysis
description: Coelophysis bauri was a small, slender Late Triassic theropod from North America and one of the best-known early dinosaurs. It had a long narrow skull, sharp teeth, a slim neck, lightweight hollow bones, long hindlimbs, grasping forelimbs, and a long balancing tail. Compared with later theropods, Coelophysis was lightly built and relatively simple in body form, showing many features of early dinosaur evolution. It was probably a quick and agile predator that fed on small vertebrates, insects, and other available prey. Large numbers of fossils from Ghost Ranch in New Mexico make Coelophysis especially important for understanding early dinosaur biology and growth.
fossils: Thousands of skeletons in a massive bonebed

name: Compsognathus
description: Compsognathus longipes was a very small Late Jurassic theropod from Europe, famous for its delicate build and historically for being one of the smallest known non-avian dinosaurs. It had a narrow skull, small sharp teeth, slender legs, grasping forelimbs, and a long tail that made up much of its body length. Compsognathus was not a baby of a larger dinosaur, but a small adult predator adapted to catching insects, lizards, and other tiny animals. Its fossils have been found in lagoonal environments, giving insight into small dinosaur life in island-like European ecosystems. Because its soft tissue is not well known, reconstructions should remain conservative and avoid excessive feathering unless presented as plausible inference from related theropods.

name: Concavenator
description: Concavenator corcovatus was an Early Cretaceous carcharodontosaurian theropod from Spain, known for the unusual raised hump or crest formed by tall vertebral spines near the hips. It had a long predatory skull, sharp teeth, three-fingered forelimbs, strong hindlimbs, and a long balancing tail. Concavenator was much smaller than giant relatives such as Giganotosaurus or Carcharodontosaurus. Its distinctive back profile makes it visually unique among theropods, although the function of the hump or ridge remains uncertain. It was likely an active predator in wetland or floodplain environments.

name: Corythosaurus
description: Corythosaurus was a Late Cretaceous lambeosaurine hadrosaur from North America, best recognized by the tall rounded helmet-like crest on top of its skull. This hollow crest was connected to the nasal passages and may have played a role in vocalization, display, or species recognition. Corythosaurus had a broad duck-billed snout, complex dental batteries for grinding vegetation, a deep herbivorous body, strong hindlimbs, sturdy forelimbs, and a long muscular tail. It could move on all fours but may also have used a bipedal posture when needed. Its crest clearly separates it from crestless hadrosaurs such as Edmontosaurus and from tube-crested relatives such as Parasaurolophus.

name: Daspletosaurus
description: Daspletosaurus torosus was a Late Cretaceous tyrannosaurid from North America and a close relative of Tyrannosaurus rex. It had a deep skull, powerful jaws, small two-fingered arms, strong hindlimbs, and a heavy predatory body. Compared with Albertosaurus and Gorgosaurus, Daspletosaurus was more robust, representing a heavier tyrannosaurine body plan. It likely hunted large herbivores such as ceratopsians and hadrosaurs. Daspletosaurus is important for understanding the evolution of later giant tyrannosaurids and the diversity of large predators before T. rex.

name: Deinonychus
description: Deinonychus antirrhopus was a medium-sized Early Cretaceous dromaeosaurid from North America and one of the most important dinosaurs in the history of paleontology. Its discovery helped support the idea that many dinosaurs were active, agile, bird-like animals rather than slow reptiles. Deinonychus had a narrow predatory skull, feathered body, long grasping forelimbs, a stiffened tail, strong hindlimbs, and a large sickle-shaped claw on the second toe of each foot. It was larger and more powerfully built than Velociraptor but smaller than Utahraptor. Deinonychus likely used its speed, claws, and jaws to subdue prey, although exact hunting behavior remains debated.

name: Dilophosaurus
description: Dilophosaurus wetherilli was an Early Jurassic theropod from North America, famous for the pair of thin bony crests running along the top of its skull. It was a relatively large but lightly built predator with a long narrow skull, slender neck, functional forelimbs, long hindlimbs, and a long balancing tail. Unlike its fictional movie portrayal, there is no evidence that Dilophosaurus had a neck frill or venom-spitting ability. Its paired cranial crests were likely used for display or species recognition rather than combat. Dilophosaurus represents an early stage in theropod evolution, combining a graceful body plan with distinctive skull ornamentation.

name: Diplodocus
description: Diplodocus was a very long Late Jurassic diplodocid sauropod from North America, famous for its small head, long slender neck, shallow body, and extremely long whip-like tail. Compared with Apatosaurus, Diplodocus was more elongated and lightly built, with a lower body profile and a much more graceful silhouette. It was a quadrupedal herbivore that likely used its peg-like teeth to strip or crop vegetation rather than chew it. Its long neck and tail helped create one of the most recognizable sauropod body plans in dinosaur paleontology. Diplodocus lived in the Morrison Formation alongside other iconic dinosaurs such as Allosaurus, Stegosaurus, Apatosaurus, and Camarasaurus.

name: Dreadnoughtus
description: Dreadnoughtus schrani was a giant Late Cretaceous titanosaur from Argentina, notable for being represented by a relatively complete skeleton for such an enormous sauropod. It had a massive torso, long neck, long tail, and strong weight-bearing limbs. Its name means “fears nothing,” reflecting its gigantic size and defensive advantage as an adult. Dreadnoughtus is especially valuable because many giant titanosaurs are known only from fragmentary remains, while this genus preserves more of the body plan.

name: Edmontosaurus
description: Edmontosaurus was a large Late Cretaceous hadrosaurid from North America and one of the best-known crestless duck-billed dinosaurs. It had a broad flattened beak, long skull, complex dental batteries, deep herbivorous torso, sturdy forelimbs, powerful hindlimbs, and a long muscular tail. Unlike Corythosaurus or Parasaurolophus, Edmontosaurus lacked a tall hollow cranial crest, giving it a plainer but very distinctive head profile. Fossil evidence, including skin impressions and exceptionally preserved specimens, has made Edmontosaurus important for understanding hadrosaur soft tissue and skin texture. It was a highly successful herbivore that lived near the end of the Cretaceous alongside Tyrannosaurus rex and Triceratops.
fossils: Numerous complete skeletons and mummified remains

name: Eoraptor
description: Eoraptor lunensis was a small Late Triassic dinosaur from Argentina and one of the earliest known dinosaurs. It had a lightweight body, long tail, slender limbs, grasping hands, and a small skull with teeth suited to a varied diet. Eoraptor lived before the major dinosaur groups became dominant and helps show what early dinosaurs may have looked like. Its simple, generalized anatomy suggests it was an agile omnivore or small predator in the Ischigualasto ecosystem, alongside other early dinosaur relatives.

name: Euoplocephalus
description: Euoplocephalus tutus was a Late Cretaceous ankylosaurid from North America, closely related to Ankylosaurus but generally better represented by fossil material. It had a wide armored body, bony osteoderms, a low skull, short sturdy limbs, and a stiff tail ending in a bony club. Unlike nodosaurids, Euoplocephalus had a true tail club. Its armor likely protected it from predators, while the tail club may have been used for defense or intraspecific combat. It is one of the classic armored dinosaurs of Alberta.

name: Gallimimus
description: Gallimimus bullatus was a large Late Cretaceous ornithomimid from Mongolia, often described as an “ostrich mimic” because of its long neck, small toothless head, lightweight body, long arms, very long running legs, and long balancing tail. It was one of the largest known ornithomimids and was probably a fast cursorial animal adapted for life in open environments. Gallimimus had a beak instead of teeth and may have been omnivorous, feeding on plants, small animals, eggs, or other available food sources. Like other ornithomimosaurs, it may have had simple feathers or filament-like body covering, although reconstructions should remain conservative. It should not be confused with raptors, which had predatory teeth and sickle claws.

name: Giganotosaurus
description: Giganotosaurus carolinii was a gigantic Late Cretaceous carcharodontosaurid theropod from Patagonia, Argentina. It was one of the largest known meat-eating dinosaurs, comparable in size to Tyrannosaurus rex but built with a different body plan. Giganotosaurus had a long, low skull, blade-like serrated teeth, three-fingered forelimbs, powerful hindlimbs, and a long tail for balance. Unlike T. rex, it did not have a short deep skull or tiny two-fingered arms; instead, it belonged to the allosauroid lineage of giant predators. Its anatomy suggests a massive predator adapted for slicing flesh from large prey, possibly including enormous sauropods that lived in the same South American ecosystems.

name: Gorgosaurus
description: Gorgosaurus libratus was a Late Cretaceous tyrannosaurid from western North America and a close relative of Albertosaurus. It had a large but relatively narrow skull, strong jaws, small two-fingered arms, long powerful legs, and a muscular tail for balance. Compared with Tyrannosaurus rex, Gorgosaurus was lighter, slimmer, and more agile, representing the gracile albertosaurine branch of tyrannosaur evolution. It likely hunted hadrosaurs, ceratopsians, and other herbivorous dinosaurs in ancient floodplain environments. Gorgosaurus is known from several well-preserved skeletons, making it one of the more informative tyrannosaurids for understanding growth, anatomy, and predator diversity before the final age of T. rex.

name: Gryposaurus
description: Gryposaurus notabilis was a Late Cretaceous hadrosaurid from North America, best known for its distinctive arched “hook-nosed” skull profile. Like other hadrosaurs, it had a broad duck-billed beak, complex dental batteries for grinding plants, a deep herbivorous torso, strong hindlimbs, sturdy forelimbs, and a long muscular tail. Unlike crest-bearing relatives such as Corythosaurus or Parasaurolophus, Gryposaurus did not have a tall hollow crest; its identity came from the raised nasal arch over the snout. It was probably a herd-living herbivore that browsed on a variety of vegetation in floodplains and coastal lowlands. Its unusual skull shape may have helped with species recognition or display.

name: Herrerasaurus
description: Herrerasaurus ischigualastensis was a Late Triassic dinosaur from Argentina and one of the earliest well-known predatory dinosaurs. It had a long skull with sharp teeth, functional grasping forelimbs, strong hindlimbs, and a long balancing tail. Herrerasaurus lived before the major dinosaur groups had fully diversified, so its anatomy appears more primitive and transitional than later Jurassic and Cretaceous theropods. It was a medium-sized bipedal predator that likely hunted small to medium-sized animals in the Ischigualasto Formation ecosystem. Because of its early position in dinosaur evolution, Herrerasaurus is important for understanding how saurischian dinosaurs and later theropod-like body plans developed.

name: Iguanodon
description: Iguanodon bernissartensis was a large Early Cretaceous ornithopod from Europe and one of the most historically important dinosaurs ever discovered. It had a robust herbivorous body, strong hindlimbs, powerful forelimbs, a beaked skull, grinding teeth, and a long stiff tail. Its most famous feature was the large conical thumb spike on each hand, which may have been used for defense, feeding, or social interaction. Iguanodon could probably move both on all fours and on its hind legs, but modern reconstructions avoid the outdated tail-dragging kangaroo posture. It was a successful plant-eating dinosaur that helps bridge the evolutionary gap between earlier ornithopods and later hadrosaur-like herbivores.

name: Kentrosaurus
description: Kentrosaurus aethiopicus was a Late Jurassic stegosaurid from East Africa, closely related to Stegosaurus but visually very different. It had a small head, low browsing posture, arched back, short forelimbs, longer hindlimbs, and a series of small plates along the front of the body that transitioned into long sharp spikes over the hips and tail. Unlike Stegosaurus, which is famous for broad upright plates, Kentrosaurus had a more spike-dominated defensive silhouette. Its tail spikes would have been important for protection against predators. Kentrosaurus was a quadrupedal herbivore that likely fed on low vegetation in the ancient Tendaguru ecosystem.

name: Lambeosaurus
description: Lambeosaurus lambei was a Late Cretaceous lambeosaurine hadrosaur from North America, known for its distinctive hatchet-shaped hollow cranial crest. Like other hadrosaurs, it had a broad duck-billed beak, complex dental batteries, strong hindlimbs, sturdy forelimbs, and a long muscular tail. Its crest may have been used for display, species recognition, or sound production. Lambeosaurus should not be confused with Corythosaurus, which had a more rounded helmet-like crest, or Parasaurolophus, which had a long backward tube crest.

name: Maiasaura
description: Maiasaura peeblesorum was a large Late Cretaceous hadrosaurid from North America, famous for fossil nesting sites that helped reveal evidence of dinosaur social and reproductive behavior. Its name means “good mother lizard,” reflecting the discovery of nests, eggs, juveniles, and adults together in large nesting colonies. Anatomically, Maiasaura had a broad duck-billed beak, dental batteries for chewing plants, a deep torso, sturdy forelimbs, powerful hindlimbs, and a long muscular tail. It lacked the dramatic hollow crests seen in lambeosaurines such as Corythosaurus or Parasaurolophus. Maiasaura was likely a herd-living herbivore that moved across floodplains and seasonal environments in large groups.

name: Majungasaurus
description: Majungasaurus crenatissimus was a Late Cretaceous abelisaurid theropod from Madagascar, known for its short deep skull, rough-textured facial bones, small cranial ornamentation, tiny forelimbs, muscular neck, and compact predatory body. Unlike Carnotaurus, it did not have large paired brow horns; instead, its skull had a rugose surface and low ornamentation on the skull roof. Majungasaurus had powerful jaws and sharp teeth, making it the dominant predator of the Maevarano Formation ecosystem. Fossil evidence suggests it may have fed on sauropods and possibly even members of its own species, although behavior should be interpreted cautiously. It is one of the best-known abelisaurids and important for understanding southern-hemisphere theropod evolution.

name: Mamenchisaurus
description: Mamenchisaurus was a Late Jurassic sauropod from China, famous for having one of the longest necks of any known dinosaur. Its body plan included a very small head, extraordinarily elongated neck, large quadrupedal torso, sturdy limbs, and a long balancing tail. Unlike Brachiosaurus, it did not have a strongly high-shouldered body with longer forelimbs; unlike Diplodocus, its defining feature was the extreme length of the neck rather than an exceptionally whip-like tail. Mamenchisaurus likely used its long neck to browse over a wide feeding area without moving its heavy body as much. Different species of Mamenchisaurus vary in size, so reconstructions should specify the species when exact proportions are required.

name: Mapusaurus
description: Mapusaurus roseae was a giant Late Cretaceous carcharodontosaurid theropod from Argentina, closely related to Giganotosaurus. It had a long low skull, blade-like serrated teeth, three-fingered forelimbs, powerful hindlimbs, and a long balancing tail. Fossils of multiple individuals found together have led to discussion about possible social behavior, although this remains uncertain. Mapusaurus lived in ecosystems that included enormous sauropods, which may have formed part of its prey base. It should be reconstructed as a long-skulled allosauroid predator, not as a tyrannosaur.

name: Masiakasaurus
description: Masiakasaurus knopfleri was a small Late Cretaceous noasaurid theropod from Madagascar, famous for its unusual forward-projecting front teeth. These teeth gave the skull a strange appearance and may have helped it catch small prey such as fish, insects, or small vertebrates. Masiakasaurus had a lightweight body, long tail, and agile limbs. Unlike Majungasaurus, the large abelisaurid predator from the same region, Masiakasaurus was small and specialized. Its unique teeth make it one of the most recognizable small theropods.

name: Megalosaurus
description: Megalosaurus bucklandii was a Middle Jurassic theropod from England and one of the most historically significant dinosaurs because it was among the first dinosaurs ever scientifically named. It was a robust meat-eating dinosaur with a large skull, sharp serrated teeth, strong hindlimbs, functional three-fingered forelimbs, and a long balancing tail. Because many fragmentary theropod fossils were once incorrectly assigned to Megalosaurus, modern reconstructions should be conservative and based on reliable material. Megalosaurus was not a tyrannosaur and should not be depicted with a boxy T. rex-like skull or tiny arms. It represents an important early-known large theropod from Middle Jurassic ecosystems of Britain.

name: Microraptor
description: Microraptor was a very small Early Cretaceous dromaeosaurid from China and one of the most important feathered dinosaurs ever discovered. It had a slender body, small toothed skull, long bony tail, clawed hands, and extensive feathers on both the forelimbs and hindlimbs, creating a distinctive four-winged appearance. Unlike larger dromaeosaurids such as Deinonychus or Velociraptor, Microraptor was tiny and likely capable of gliding or controlled aerial movement between trees or elevated surfaces. Fossil evidence preserves detailed feather impressions, making it crucial for understanding the relationship between non-avian dinosaurs and birds. It should not be reconstructed as a naked scaly raptor or as a modern bird with a short tail.

name: Mononykus
description: Mononykus olecranus was a small Late Cretaceous alvarezsaurid from Mongolia, famous for its extremely reduced forelimbs ending in one large functional claw. It had long slender legs, a lightweight body, small head, and likely feather-like covering. Mononykus was not a raptor or a baby theropod; it belonged to a specialized group of small maniraptoran dinosaurs. Its powerful single-clawed arms may have been used for digging into insect nests or rotting wood, suggesting an insect-eating lifestyle. It is one of the strangest small theropods known.

name: Muttaburrasaurus
description: Muttaburrasaurus langdoni was a large Early Cretaceous ornithopod from Australia, best recognized by its unusual rounded, bulbous snout. It had a sturdy herbivorous body, powerful hindlimbs, usable forelimbs, a long stiff tail, and a beaked mouth adapted for feeding on plants. Unlike Iguanodon, it did not have large thumb spikes, and unlike hadrosaurs, it did not have a true duck-billed skull or hollow cranial crest. The enlarged nasal region may have been connected to sound production, display, or other soft-tissue structures, although this remains uncertain. Muttaburrasaurus is one of the best-known Australian dinosaurs and represents a distinctive branch of large Gondwanan ornithopods.

name: Nigersaurus
description: Nigersaurus taqueti was a strange Early Cretaceous sauropod from Niger, famous for its wide squared muzzle and hundreds of small replacement teeth. Unlike tall-browsing sauropods, Nigersaurus had a low head posture and was likely adapted for grazing or cropping low vegetation. Its skull was very lightweight and specialized, giving it one of the most unusual feeding adaptations among sauropods. Despite internet fame for its teeth, it was a real and scientifically important rebbachisaurid sauropod.

name: Nodosaurus
description: Nodosaurus textilis was a Cretaceous armored dinosaur from North America and the namesake of the nodosaurid family. It had a low quadrupedal body covered with bony armor plates and nodules, but unlike ankylosaurids it did not have a tail club. Nodosaurus likely relied on its armor and possibly shoulder or side protection rather than a clubbed tail. It was a slow-moving herbivore that fed on low vegetation. Because its remains are incomplete, reconstructions often use better-known nodosaurids for comparison.

name: Ouranosaurus
description: Ouranosaurus nigeriensis was a large Early Cretaceous iguanodontian herbivore from North Africa, famous for the tall neural spines along its back. These elongated spines may have supported a sail-like structure or a thicker soft-tissue ridge, although the exact appearance is still debated. Ouranosaurus had a broad herbivorous beak, strong hindlimbs, usable forelimbs, a long balancing tail, and a body plan generally similar to other iguanodontians. Unlike Spinosaurus, it was not a carnivorous theropod and did not have a crocodile-like skull. Its distinctive raised back profile makes it one of the most visually recognizable ornithopods from Cretaceous Africa.

name: Oviraptor
description: Oviraptor philoceratops was a small Late Cretaceous oviraptorosaur from Mongolia, known for its short deep skull, toothless beak, bird-like body, and likely feathered covering. Its name means “egg thief,” but this interpretation is now considered misleading because related fossils show oviraptorosaurs brooding their own nests rather than stealing eggs. Oviraptor had strong jaws, long arms, clawed hands, slender legs, and a relatively long feathered tail. It was probably omnivorous, feeding on a mixture of plants, small animals, eggs, or hard-shelled food depending on availability. Because some famous crested oviraptorosaur reconstructions are based on relatives such as Citipati, Oviraptor should be reconstructed conservatively.

name: Pachycephalosaurus
description: Pachycephalosaurus wyomingensis was a Late Cretaceous ornithischian from North America, famous for its thick rounded skull dome. The dome was surrounded by smaller bony knobs and blunt spikes, giving the head a very distinctive profile. Pachycephalosaurus was a bipedal dinosaur with a compact body, short forelimbs, strong hindlimbs, a stiff balancing tail, and a small beaked snout. The function of its dome is still debated: it may have been used for display, species recognition, flank-butting, head-butting, or some combination of these behaviors. Because much of the body is reconstructed from related pachycephalosaurs, its postcranial proportions should be treated with some caution.
fossils: Nearly complete skull and partial skeletons

name: Pachyrhinosaurus
description: Pachyrhinosaurus was a Late Cretaceous centrosaurine ceratopsian from North America, best known for its large rough nasal boss instead of a tall nose horn. It had a powerful parrot-like beak, heavy skull, compact frill, smaller brow bosses, strong shoulders, and a massive quadrupedal body. Unlike Triceratops, it did not have long brow horns, and unlike Styracosaurus, it did not have a huge nasal horn with dramatic frill spikes. The thickened nasal boss may have been covered in keratin and could have played a role in display, combat, or species recognition. Pachyrhinosaurus was likely a herd-living herbivore adapted to northern Late Cretaceous environments.
fossils: Multiple complete skeletons in massive bonebeds

name: Parasaurolophus
description: Parasaurolophus walkeri was a Late Cretaceous lambeosaurine hadrosaur from North America, famous for its long backward-projecting hollow cranial crest. This tubular crest was connected to the nasal passages and may have been used for sound production, display, species recognition, or other biological functions. Parasaurolophus had a broad duck-billed beak, complex dental batteries for processing plants, sturdy forelimbs, powerful hindlimbs, and a long muscular tail. It could move on all fours but may also have shifted into a bipedal posture when needed. Its long crest clearly separates it from Corythosaurus, Lambeosaurus, Edmontosaurus, and other hadrosaurs.

name: Patagotitan
description: Patagotitan mayorum was a gigantic Late Cretaceous titanosaur from Patagonia, Argentina, and is often listed among the largest land animals ever discovered. It had an enormous body, long neck, long tail, and powerful columnar limbs adapted to support extreme body mass. Although its exact size is still estimated from incomplete material, the known fossils show a truly colossal sauropod. Patagotitan is important for understanding the evolution of giant titanosaurs in South America.

name: Plateosaurus
description: Plateosaurus engelhardti was a Late Triassic sauropodomorph from Europe and one of the best-known early relatives of the giant sauropods. It had a long neck, small head, large grasping hands, strong hindlimbs, and a long tail. Unlike later sauropods, Plateosaurus was not fully quadrupedal and may have moved primarily on two legs while feeding on plants. Its fossils are abundant, making it important for understanding early dinosaur growth, herbivory, and the evolutionary path toward enormous sauropods.

name: Protoceratops
description: Protoceratops andrewsi was a small Late Cretaceous protoceratopsid from Mongolia, often described as an early relative of larger horned dinosaurs such as Triceratops. It had a proportionally large skull, strong parrot-like beak, modest neck frill, compact quadrupedal body, short limbs, and a medium-length tail. Unlike later ceratopsids, Protoceratops lacked large brow horns and did not have a huge nose horn. It was a low-slung herbivore adapted to dry desert-steppe environments, where it likely fed on tough vegetation. Numerous fossils, including growth stages and famous specimens preserved with Velociraptor, make Protoceratops one of the best-known small ceratopsians.
fossils: Hundreds of complete skeletons in all growth stages

name: Psittacosaurus
description: Psittacosaurus mongoliensis was a small Early Cretaceous ceratopsian from Asia and an early relative of later horned dinosaurs. Its name means “parrot lizard” because of its strong beaked skull. Unlike Triceratops or Protoceratops, Psittacosaurus was mostly bipedal and lacked a large frill or horns. Exceptional fossils preserve skin details and tail bristle-like structures, making it one of the most informative small ornithischians. It likely fed on low vegetation, seeds, and tough plant material.

name: Saurolophus
description: Saurolophus osborni was a Late Cretaceous saurolophine hadrosaur known for its backward-projecting solid cranial crest. Unlike Parasaurolophus, its crest was not a long hollow tube, and unlike Edmontosaurus, it was not completely crestless. Saurolophus had a broad beak, dental batteries for chewing plants, a deep body, strong hindlimbs, sturdy forelimbs, and a long tail. It was a successful herbivore in Late Cretaceous ecosystems and is important for comparing crest evolution among hadrosaurs.

name: Sauropelta
description: Sauropelta edwardsorum was an Early Cretaceous nodosaurid from North America, famous for its heavy armor and long shoulder spikes. It had a low, broad quadrupedal body, bony plates across its back, strong limbs, a beaked mouth, and no tail club. The large shoulder spikes helped distinguish it from ankylosaurids such as Ankylosaurus or Euoplocephalus. Sauropelta was a slow-moving herbivore that likely relied on armor and defensive posture to survive attacks from predators. It is one of the best-known nodosaurids from North America.

name: Sinosauropteryx
description: Sinosauropteryx prima was a small Early Cretaceous theropod from China and one of the first non-avian dinosaurs discovered with clear fossil evidence of filament-like feathers. It had a slender body, long tail, small skull, sharp teeth, and simple fuzzy covering rather than modern flight feathers. Fossil evidence even preserves hints of color patterning, including a banded tail in some interpretations. Sinosauropteryx is extremely important for understanding the origin of feathers and the close relationship between dinosaurs and birds.

name: Spinosaurus
description: Spinosaurus aegyptiacus was a gigantic Late Cretaceous spinosaurid from North Africa, best known for its long crocodile-like snout, conical fish-catching teeth, tall dorsal sail, powerful forelimbs, relatively short hindlimbs, and broad paddle-like tail. Unlike Tyrannosaurus or Giganotosaurus, Spinosaurus was strongly associated with river and wetland environments and probably fed heavily on fish and other aquatic or shoreline prey. Modern discoveries have changed its reconstruction significantly, especially by emphasizing its semi-aquatic adaptations and unusual tail. However, the exact degree to which it swam or hunted underwater remains debated. Its fossil history is complicated because early Egyptian material was destroyed during World War II, making cautious reconstruction important.

name: Stegosaurus
description: Stegosaurus stenops was a large Late Jurassic stegosaurid from North America, instantly recognizable by the two rows of large upright plates along its back and the spiked tail weapon known as a thagomizer. It had a very small head, low browsing posture, short forelimbs, taller hindlimbs, arched back, bulky body, and a long muscular tail. The plates may have been used for display, species recognition, thermoregulation, or a combination of functions, but their exact purpose remains debated. The tail spikes were likely an important defensive weapon against predators such as Allosaurus. Stegosaurus was a slow-moving quadrupedal herbivore and one of the most iconic dinosaurs from the Morrison Formation.

name: Struthiomimus
description: Struthiomimus altus was a Late Cretaceous ornithomimid from North America, with an ostrich-like body plan adapted for speed. It had a small toothless head with a beak, long slender neck, lightweight torso, long arms, very long running legs, three-toed feet, and a long balancing tail. Struthiomimus was not a raptor and lacked the enlarged sickle claw and predatory teeth of dromaeosaurids. It may have been omnivorous, feeding on plants, small animals, eggs, insects, or other available resources. Like other ornithomimosaurs, it may have had simple feathers or filament-like covering, although reconstructions should remain conservative and avoid making it look like a modern ostrich.

name: Styracosaurus
description: Styracosaurus albertensis was a Late Cretaceous centrosaurine ceratopsian from North America, famous for its large nose horn and dramatic spikes projecting from the edge of its frill. It had a strong parrot-like beak, deep skull, short frill, powerful shoulders, heavy quadrupedal body, and sturdy limbs. Unlike Triceratops, Styracosaurus did not have two long brow horns; its skull display was dominated by the nasal horn and long frill spikes. These ornaments may have been used for display, species recognition, and defense. Styracosaurus lived in rich floodplain ecosystems alongside other ceratopsians, hadrosaurs, tyrannosaurids, and armored dinosaurs.

name: Supersaurus
description: Supersaurus vivianae was an extremely long Late Jurassic diplodocid sauropod from North America. It had a very long neck, elongated body, long tail, and relatively slender diplodocid proportions. Supersaurus is often discussed as one of the longest dinosaurs, although its exact total length depends on reconstruction. Unlike bulky titanosaurs, its body was defined more by extreme length than by massive weight. It lived in Morrison Formation ecosystems alongside other sauropods, stegosaurs, and large theropod predators.

name: Tarbosaurus
description: Tarbosaurus bataar was a large Late Cretaceous tyrannosaurid from Mongolia, closely related to Tyrannosaurus rex. It had a large skull, powerful jaws, tiny two-fingered arms, strong hindlimbs, and a long counterbalancing tail. Compared with T. rex, Tarbosaurus had some differences in skull proportions and lived in Asian ecosystems dominated by dinosaurs such as hadrosaurs, ankylosaurs, and sauropods. It was probably the apex predator of the Nemegt Formation. Tarbosaurus is one of the best-known Asian tyrannosaurids and a key comparison for T. rex evolution.

name: Therizinosaurus
description: Therizinosaurus cheloniformis was a large Late Cretaceous therizinosaurid from Mongolia, famous for its enormous scythe-like hand claws, long neck, small head, broad hips, and deep pot-bellied body. Although it was a theropod, it was very different from predatory theropods such as Tyrannosaurus or Velociraptor. Therizinosaurus was likely herbivorous or primarily plant-eating, using its long neck and huge claws to pull branches, strip vegetation, defend itself, or display. Its body was probably covered in simple feathers or filament-like plumage, based on evidence from related therizinosaurs. Because much of its skeleton is incomplete, reconstructions should remain cautious, but its giant claws make it one of the most distinctive dinosaurs ever discovered.

name: Torosaurus
description: Torosaurus latus was a large Late Cretaceous chasmosaurine ceratopsian from North America, closely related to Triceratops. It had two long brow horns, a nose horn, a powerful beak, and an especially long frill with large openings. Torosaurus has been involved in debate over whether it represents a distinct genus or a mature growth stage of Triceratops, although many studies continue to treat it separately. It was a large quadrupedal herbivore that lived in the same final Cretaceous ecosystems as T. rex.

name: Torvosaurus
description: Torvosaurus tanneri was a large Late Jurassic megalosaurid theropod from North America. It had a massive skull, powerful jaws, large serrated teeth, strong forelimbs with large claws, robust hindlimbs, and a long balancing tail. Torvosaurus lived in the Morrison Formation alongside Allosaurus, Ceratosaurus, Stegosaurus, and many sauropods. Unlike Allosaurus, it belonged to the megalosaurid lineage and had a heavier, more powerfully built skull and body. It was probably one of the largest predators in its ecosystem, hunting or scavenging large herbivorous dinosaurs.

name: Triceratops
description: Triceratops horridus was a massive Late Cretaceous ceratopsian from North America and one of the last non-avian dinosaurs before the end-Cretaceous extinction. It had a huge skull, two long brow horns, a smaller nose horn, a large solid neck frill, a strong parrot-like beak, powerful shoulders, and a heavy quadrupedal body. Unlike Styracosaurus, it lacked long frill spikes, and unlike Chasmosaurus, its frill was shorter and more solid-looking. Triceratops likely used its horns and frill for display, species recognition, defense, and possibly combat with rivals. It lived alongside Tyrannosaurus rex in the Hell Creek ecosystem and was one of the dominant large herbivores of its time.

name: Troodon
description: Troodon formosus is a historically famous name for a small Late Cretaceous troodontid-like dinosaur, but its scientific status is debated. Many fossils once assigned to Troodon have since been reclassified into other troodontid genera, so reconstructions should be presented carefully. In a conservative interpretation, Troodon can be shown as a small, bird-like, feathered maniraptoran with large eyes, a narrow skull, small teeth, long legs, grasping arms, a long tail, and an enlarged second-toe claw. It was probably an agile omnivore or small-prey hunter rather than a large predator. Because the name is taxonomically complicated, Troodon is best treated as an uncertain but historically important troodontid entry.

name: Tuojiangosaurus
description: Tuojiangosaurus multispinus was a Late Jurassic stegosaurid from China, closely related to Stegosaurus but with a more pointed and angular armor profile. It had a small narrow head, low browsing posture, arched back, short forelimbs, longer hindlimbs, paired rows of pointed dorsal plates, and a spiked tail. Unlike Stegosaurus, which is famous for broad leaf-shaped plates, Tuojiangosaurus had narrower, sharper-looking plates along the back. Its tail spikes probably served as a defensive weapon against predators. Tuojiangosaurus was a quadrupedal herbivore that fed on low vegetation and represents one of the best-known stegosaurs from Asia.

name: Tyrannosaurus Rex
description: Tyrannosaurus rex was a gigantic Late Cretaceous tyrannosaurid from North America and one of the most powerful terrestrial predators ever known. It had an enormous deep skull, thick bone-crushing teeth, a muscular neck, massive torso, huge hindlimbs, a long heavy tail, and very small but strong two-fingered arms. Unlike Giganotosaurus or Carcharodontosaurus, T. rex had a short, deep skull built for an extremely powerful bite rather than a long blade-like skull for slicing. Modern reconstructions often show closed-mouth teeth covered by soft tissue rather than permanently exposed like a crocodile. T. rex lived in the Hell Creek ecosystem and likely hunted and scavenged large herbivores such as Triceratops and Edmontosaurus.

name: Utahraptor
description: Utahraptor ostrommaysi was a giant Early Cretaceous dromaeosaurid from North America and one of the largest known “raptor” dinosaurs. It was much bigger and more powerfully built than Velociraptor or Deinonychus, with a stocky body, strong hindlimbs, long grasping forelimbs, a stiff balancing tail, and a large sickle-shaped claw on the second toe of each foot. As a dromaeosaurid, it was likely feathered, although direct feather impressions are not known for this species. Utahraptor should not be imagined as a naked movie monster or a scaled-up Velociraptor; it was a heavy, ground-dwelling, bird-related predator. Its fossils help show how diverse and large dromaeosaurids could become.
fossils: Partial skeletons and multiple bonebed specimens

name: Velociraptor
description: Velociraptor mongoliensis was a small Late Cretaceous dromaeosaurid from Mongolia, very different from the oversized scaly raptors often shown in movies. It was a lightly built, feathered predator with a long low skull, narrow snout, sharp teeth, long forelimbs, a stiffened tail, and an enlarged sickle claw on each foot. Direct fossil evidence from the forearm supports the presence of feathers, so accurate reconstructions should show it as a feathered animal. Velociraptor likely hunted small animals and may have scavenged when possible in arid desert-steppe environments. It was closer in size to a turkey or large dog than to the human-sized raptors of popular fiction.

name: Yutyrannus
description: Yutyrannus huali was a large Early Cretaceous tyrannosauroid from China and one of the largest known dinosaurs with direct evidence of feather-like covering. It had a long skull, strong legs, three-fingered hands, and a body covered with filamentous feathers or protofeathers. Unlike Tyrannosaurus rex, it was not a late giant tyrannosaurid with tiny two-fingered arms. Yutyrannus is important because it shows that large tyrannosauroids could retain extensive feathering, especially in cooler Early Cretaceous environments.

name: Zuul
description: Zuul crurivastator was a Late Cretaceous ankylosaurid from North America, named after the monster Zuul from Ghostbusters because of its armored skull. It is known from an exceptional specimen preserving the skull, body armor, and tail club. Like other ankylosaurids, Zuul had a wide low body, bony osteoderms, sturdy limbs, and a stiff tail ending in a heavy club. Its fossils provide rare evidence for armor arrangement and possible injuries, making it important for understanding ankylosaur defense and behavior.
